title: The Water That Keeps Coming Back
blurb: No water on Earth is new. The rain in your yard has been an ocean, a cloud, and a dinosaur's drink, and it is still going around.

blocks.prompt: Where the Puddle Went
blocks.text: Look at a puddle on a warm day. Come back later and it is gone. The puddle did not go away. The sun warmed it until it turned into water vapor, and vapor is so small you cannot see it. It floated up into the sky. High up, the air is cold. The vapor cooled and turned back into tiny drops. Millions of drops together make a cloud. The drops bump into each other and grow. When a drop is too heavy for the air to hold, it falls. That is rain. The rain lands, and it makes a new puddle.

blocks.prompt: Where the Puddle Goes
blocks.text: Every puddle has somewhere to be. On a warm day the sun pours energy into the water. The fastest bits of water break free from the surface and drift away as water vapor, a gas so thin and clear that it is invisible. Scientists call this evaporation. Plants do it too. Roots pull water up from the soil, and leaves let it slip out into the air. One big oak tree can send tens of thousands of gallons of water into the sky in a single year. High above the ground the air is much colder, and cold air cannot hold as much vapor. So the vapor turns back into liquid. It sticks to specks of dust and salt floating in the air, and each speck grows a tiny drop around it. Billions of those drops hanging together are what you see as a cloud. The drops bump, join, and get heavier. When they are too heavy to float, gravity takes over and they fall as rain or snow. The water soaks into the ground, or runs into a creek, and the creek runs to the sea. Then the sun starts the whole thing over again.

blocks.prompt: The Oldest Water You Will Ever Drink
blocks.text: Fill a glass of water and you are holding something ancient. Almost every drop of water on Earth has been here for billions of years, and none of it is new. It has been ocean, cloud, river, ice, and rain, over and over, in a loop that has never once stopped. The engine of that loop is the sun. Sunlight heats the ocean and gives some water molecules enough energy to escape into the air as vapor, an invisible gas. This is evaporation, and the ocean supplies most of it. Something clever happens on the way up. Salt cannot evaporate. It stays behind in the sea, so the vapor that rises is pure fresh water. The sky is the largest distillery on the planet. Higher up, the air is colder and holds less vapor, so the water condenses onto floating specks of dust, smoke, and sea salt flung up by breaking waves. The droplets that form are so small that a million of them would barely fill one raindrop. Clouds are those droplets, not vapor. If you can see it, it is already liquid again. Droplets collide, merge, and grow until the air can no longer hold them, and then they fall as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. What comes down does not stay put. Some runs across the land into rivers and back to the sea. Some soaks into rock and becomes groundwater, where it may sit for thousands of years. Some freezes into a glacier and waits. On average a water molecule spends about nine days in the atmosphere, but roughly three thousand years in the ocean. The water in your glass is on one lap of a very long race, and you are a short stop along the way.

blocks.prompt: The Sky Is a Distillery
blocks.text: Ask where the rain comes from and the honest answer is: from everywhere it has already been. Earth's water is a closed loop of about 1.4 billion cubic kilometers, and the total barely changes. What changes is where the water sits, and how long it stays. The sun runs the loop. Roughly 86 percent of the vapor entering the atmosphere lifts off the ocean. The rest comes from lakes, soil, and plants, which draw water up through their roots and release it from their leaves in a process called transpiration. Evaporation is fussy about what it takes. Salt, minerals, and most pollutants cannot leave with the vapor, so they stay behind. Every cloud is therefore a batch of distilled water, and the atmosphere is the largest purification plant that has ever existed. Evaporation also moves energy. Turning liquid water into vapor takes a great deal of heat, and that heat travels along with the vapor like hidden luggage. When the vapor cools and condenses into cloud droplets, the heat is released into the surrounding air. This is why storms have power. A hurricane is, at heart, an enormous engine running on warm ocean water condensing at altitude. Condensation needs a surface to build on. Vapor gathers on microscopic specks of dust, smoke, pollen, and sea salt, each speck seeding a droplet about a hundredth of a millimeter across. It takes roughly a million such droplets to assemble one raindrop, which is why a cloud can hang overhead for hours without dropping a thing. Then comes the part people forget. Water that falls does not simply wait around to evaporate again. It has choices. It may run off into a river and reach the sea within days. It may soak into porous rock and become groundwater, resting there for centuries. It may lock into an ice sheet and hold still for a hundred thousand years. Scientists call this residence time, and it is the difference between a puddle and a glacier. Here is the catch. About 97 percent of Earth's water is salt water. Most of the fresh remainder is frozen solid or buried deep. Less than one percent is liquid fresh water we can actually reach, and in places like the Great Plains, people pump it out of ancient aquifers faster than rain can refill them. The water never runs out. It simply refuses to be where we want it, when we want it, and no amount of asking will hurry the cycle along.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Water That Keeps Coming Back

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Water has been cycling for roughly 4 billion years
Latent heat: evaporation stores it, condensation releases it
The Amazon's flying rivers carry rain thousands of kilometers
Cloud droplet: about a hundredth of a millimeter wide
The Ogallala Aquifer is drained faster than it refills
Less than 1 percent of Earth's water is fresh and reachable

blocks.prompt: The Loop That Cannot Be Broken, Only Moved
blocks.text: Nothing about the water cycle is new. That is the first thing to understand about it, and the strangest. The oceans, the rain, the ice, and the water inside your own cells have been circling this planet for roughly four billion years, and the total amount has hardly budged. There is no factory making more of it. Every glass you have ever drunk was borrowed. The loop runs on sunlight and gravity, which is a suspiciously short list of ingredients for something so large. Sunlight strikes the ocean and hands energy to the molecules at the surface. A few of them collect enough to break away entirely and rise as vapor, an invisible gas. About 86 percent of the water entering the atmosphere leaves the ocean this way. The remainder evaporates from lakes and soil, or exits through plants, which pull water up from their roots and breathe it out through pores in their leaves. That last route is called transpiration, and it is no rounding error. A single large oak can release tens of thousands of gallons in a year, and the Amazon rainforest exhales so much vapor that scientists describe the result as flying rivers, airborne flows that deliver rain to farmland thousands of kilometers downwind. Evaporation is selective, and this is the quiet miracle of the whole system. Salt does not rise. Neither do most minerals or pollutants. Only the water leaves, so what condenses in the sky is distilled, and the sea stays salty precisely because the fresh water keeps departing without it. The atmosphere purifies an entire planet's water supply for free, continuously, and has done so since long before there was anyone around to be grateful. Rising vapor also smuggles energy. Evaporating water absorbs a large amount of heat, which travels invisibly with the gas until the vapor cools, condenses, and releases it again. This is why a hurricane is not merely a wind event but a heat engine: warm ocean water evaporates, condenses at altitude, dumps its stored heat into the storm, and the storm uses that energy to haul up still more water. Condensation needs something to cling to. Droplets form on microscopic specks of dust, smoke, pollen, and sea salt thrown up by breaking waves. Each droplet is roughly a hundredth of a millimeter wide, and about a million of them must collide and merge before a single raindrop is heavy enough to fall. Clouds float not because water is light but because the droplets are small enough for rising air to carry. What falls then scatters into wildly different futures. Some water reaches the sea within a week. Some soaks into porous rock and becomes groundwater that will not see daylight for ten thousand years. Some freezes into an ice sheet and outwaits entire civilizations. Hydrologists call this residence time: about nine days in the atmosphere, roughly three thousand years in the ocean, far longer underground. Which brings us to the uncomfortable arithmetic. About 97 percent of Earth's water is salt. Most of the rest is frozen solid or locked deep in rock. Less than one percent is liquid fresh water within human reach, and much of that is being withdrawn faster than the cycle returns it. The Ogallala Aquifer beneath the Great Plains holds water that fell before farming was invented, and irrigation is drawing it down in decades. So the cycle is not fragile. It will outlast us without effort. What is fragile is our assumption that it will keep delivering to the same address. The water is never destroyed. It is only ever somewhere else.
